content: Patients who require prolonged bladder catheterization often experience significant discomfort and inconvenience. Extended catheter use is associated with an increased risk of infections, tissue erosion, higher costs per patient, and a greater demand for intensive nursing care. Shorter durations of postoperative bladder catheterization have been tested in cases of simple obstetric fistula and have demonstrated effectiveness in promoting complete healing, improving patient comfort, and potentially reducing the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infections. The surgical repair of obstetric fistulae is contingent upon the availability of operating rooms, sufficient recovery bed space, skilled surgeons with specialized training, and, in many cases, financial support from donors to fund both the operations and postoperative care. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), the demand for fistula repair services far exceeds the available human and infrastructural capacity of the healthcare system. Reducing the duration of bladder catheterization could lead to shorter hospital stays, thereby enabling more fistula patients to be treated within existing facilities. Evidence-based guidance on the optimal duration of bladder catheterization following surgery can significantly enhance the health and well-being of women with fistula. However, decisions regarding fistula care are often based on individual surgeon preferences rather than robust research evidence. Despite the limited availability of evidence-based data on fistula management, there is a pressing need to establish formal recommendations to improve outcomes for affected women. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a guideline focused on the duration of bladder catheterization after the surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula. This intervention can be implemented by appropriately trained surgeons, including those with less experience, and has direct health and cost implications, particularly in LMICs. The guideline aims to provide a sustainable framework for implementing this intervention, ultimately alleviating the suffering of many women with simple obstetric urinary fistula. The primary audience for this guideline includes healthcare professionals, particularly fistula surgeons and nurses involved in postoperative care for women undergoing surgery for obstetric urinary fistula. Additionally, the guideline is intended to assist national and local policymakers, as well as staff from non-governmental and other organizations involved in fistula care services. The guideline specifically addresses women diagnosed with simple obstetric urinary fistula, defined as a vesicovaginal fistula caused by obstructed labor. It does not cover complex obstetric fistulae or those unrelated to obstetric causes. The guideline was developed using WHO’s standardized procedures for evidence-informed policymaking. The process included identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. The development process involved four main groups: the WHO Steering Group, the Guideline Development Group (GDG), the External Review Group (ERG), and the Systematic Review Team. The WHO Steering Group, composed of staff from the Departments of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) and Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA), managed the entire guideline development process. They drafted the initial scope, identified priority questions in PICO format (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome), and selected members for the GDG, ERG, and Systematic Review Team. The Steering Group also supervised evidence synthesis, organized the GDG meeting, finalized the guideline document, and managed its dissemination and implementation. The GDG consisted of 11 external experts and stakeholders from various WHO regions, including representatives of women affected by the recommendations. The group ensured geographic and gender representation and addressed potential conflicts of interest. They contributed to drafting the guideline scope, prioritizing outcomes, appraising evidence, and formulating the final recommendation. The ERG, comprising four technical experts with experience in evidence-based fistula care, reviewed the final guideline document for factual accuracy, clarity, and contextual relevance. They did not alter the recommendations formulated by the GDG. The Systematic Review Team, led by guideline methodologists, conducted a systematic review to gather evidence on the priority question. The review followed standard methods recommended by the Cochrane Handbook and PRISMA guidelines. The evidence was appraised using the GRADE methodology, which assessed study design limitations, inconsistency of results, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. The findings were summarized in GRADE evidence profiles, which informed the recommendation. The recommendation was formulated using the GRADE framework, considering the balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences, and cost/resource implications. The draft recommendation and supporting documents were reviewed and finalized during a Technical Consultation held at WHO headquarters in Geneva in May 2017. All external contributors were required to declare relevant interests before participating in the guideline development process, in accordance with WHO regulations.
